title: Time Needed to Buy Tickets
description: Brute force to optimized: a literal round-robin queue simulation versus a direct O(n) per-person contribution formula.

blocks.text: n people are queuing to buy tickets (person 0 at the front, person n-1 at the back). tickets[i] is how many tickets person i wants. Each person takes exactly 1 second to buy ONE ticket; if they still need more, they go to the BACK of the line instantly. Once a person has bought all their tickets, they leave. Return the total time (in seconds) for the person originally at position k to finish buying ALL of their tickets.

blocks.caption: A direct queue simulation (1 second per ticket, requeue at the back if more tickets are still needed) directly matches the problem's description

{"headers":["Signal in the problem","Pattern it points to"],"rows":[["A literal queue is described (people cycling to the back of the line)","A direct queue simulation naturally and correctly models the process"],["Only person k's FINISH time matters, not the full simulation","Each OTHER person's exact contribution to that finish time can be computed directly, without simulating every second"]]}

blocks.text: Person k finishes exactly when they have bought their LAST ticket; every OTHER person contributes exactly as many seconds to the total elapsed time as tickets they buy BEFORE person k finishes, which depends on whether they are originally ahead of or behind k in line.

blocks.title: Analogy: Counting How Many Times Everyone Ahead of (and Behind) You Gets Served Before You're Done
blocks.text: Imagine a repeating round-robin line where everyone buys one ticket per turn and rejoins the back if they need more. To know exactly when a SPECIFIC person finishes, count: for everyone originally AHEAD of (or at) that person, how many tickets do they buy in every round UP TO AND INCLUDING that person's very last round; for everyone originally BEHIND that person, how many tickets do they buy in every round EXCEPT that final one (since the line has already finished by the time it would reach them again).

blocks.caption: A person ahead of (or at) k contributes up to tickets[k] seconds; a person behind k contributes up to tickets[k]-1 seconds, since k finishes before the line reaches them in that final round

blocks.content: {"headers":["Person","Position vs k=2","Contribution","Why"],"rows":[["0 (2 tickets)","Before k","min(2, tickets[2]=2) = 2","Buys both tickets, each within a round that k also participates in"],["1 (3 tickets)","Before k","min(3, tickets[2]=2) = 2","Only 2 of their 3 tickets are bought before/during k's final round"],["2 (2 tickets, this IS k)","At k","min(2, tickets[2]=2) = 2","k buys exactly their own 2 tickets"],["Answer","2+2+2 = 6","-","Matches the expected result"]]}

blocks.text: Before literally simulating the queue second by second (correct, but doing more work than strictly needed since only person k's finish time is asked for), notice that each OTHER person's exact contribution to that finish time can be computed directly, based on whether they are ahead of or behind k.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: Person k finishes on the round where they buy their tickets[k]-th (final) ticket; that round is the LAST round that matters for computing the total elapsed time.

Observation 2: A person originally AT OR BEFORE position k in line is served BEFORE k in every round, including k's very last round; such a person contributes exactly min(their own ticket count, tickets[k]) seconds, since they cannot buy MORE tickets than k does (rounds beyond k's last round do not count), but they DO get to participate in every round up through k's last one.

Observation 3: A person originally AFTER position k contributes exactly min(their own ticket count, tickets[k] - 1) seconds instead, since by the time the line would cycle back around to them in k's FINAL round, k has ALREADY finished and left, so that final round never actually happens for them.

Observation 4: Summing every person's individual contribution (computed directly via this min() formula, no simulation needed) gives the exact total time for k to finish.

This is a direct O(n) computation: each person's contribution to k's finish time is min(their tickets, tickets[k]) if positioned at or before k, or min(their tickets, tickets[k]-1) if positioned after k.
Directly simulate the queue: each second, the person at the front buys one ticket and either leaves (if done) or rejoins the back of the line; stop the moment person k finishes.

items: Maintain a queue of person indices, initialized in order, and a "remaining tickets" count per person.
Each second, dequeue the front person, decrement their remaining count, and either stop (if this was person k finishing) or requeue them (if they still need more tickets).

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: A queue directly and literally models the described process, making correctness easy to verify against the problem statement.
Stopping the moment person k finishes avoids simulating any unnecessary seconds beyond what is actually asked for.

blocks.text: Correctly finds person k's finish time, since it directly and faithfully simulates the exact process described.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n * max(tickets)), since the simulation runs for as many seconds as it takes person k to finish, potentially requeuing many people multiple times.
Space: O(n), for the queue and remaining-count tracking.

Limitation: simulating every single second is unnecessary when only ONE person's finish time is needed; each other person's exact contribution can be computed directly in O(1), without ever simulating individual seconds.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text: The brute force simulates every second explicitly. Instead, recognize that each person's contribution to k's finish time depends only on their POSITION relative to k and their own ticket count: someone at or before k contributes min(their tickets, tickets[k]); someone after k contributes min(their tickets, tickets[k] - 1), since k finishes and leaves before the line would cycle back to them one final time. Summing these direct contributions across all n people gives the answer in one pass.
For each person i: if i <= k, add min(tickets[i], tickets[k]) to the total; otherwise, add min(tickets[i], tickets[k] - 1). Return the total after processing all n people.
Directly compute each person's contribution to k's finish time based on their position relative to k, summing in a single O(n) pass.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n), a single pass over all people.
Space: O(1) extra.

In the round-robin process, everyone gets EXACTLY one turn per "round" (one pass around the current line), in their original relative order. By the time person k buys their FINAL ticket (finishing), everyone originally BEFORE (or at) k in line has had a chance to participate in that SAME final round; everyone originally AFTER k, however, would only get their turn in that round AFTER k, but k has ALREADY finished and left by then, so that round never actually happens for them. This precisely explains the min(tickets[k]) vs. min(tickets[k]-1) distinction.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Case","What happens"],"rows":[["Person i is at or before k's original position","Contributes min(tickets[i], tickets[k]) seconds, participating in every round up through and including k's final one"],["Person i is after k's original position","Contributes min(tickets[i], tickets[k] - 1) seconds, missing out on k's final round entirely"],["Person i needs FEWER tickets than the cap allows","Contributes exactly their own full ticket count, since they finish (and stop contributing rounds) before the cap is even reached"]]}

items: The i <= k check directly captures "originally at or before k's position in line," which determines which of the two contribution formulas applies.
Using min() naturally caps each person's contribution at however many rounds actually occur, without needing separate conditional logic for "did this person finish early."
No queue or explicit simulation is needed at all, since every person's contribution is now a direct, independent O(1) computation.

blocks.text: When a round-robin queue simulation only asks about ONE specific participant's finish time, each OTHER participant's exact contribution can often be computed directly (based on their position relative to the target and their own count), entirely avoiding a literal step-by-step simulation.

items: Using the SAME formula (min(tickets[i], tickets[k])) for everyone, missing the crucial -1 adjustment for people positioned AFTER k.
Getting the position comparison backward (using < instead of <= for "at or before k"), which would incorrectly exclude k's own contribution.
Defaulting to a full queue simulation when the problem only asks about one specific person's finish time, missing the more efficient direct-computation opportunity.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Edge case","Expected behavior"],"rows":[["k = 0 (the very first person)","Contributes their full ticket count directly; everyone else uses the \"after k\" formula"],["Everyone wants exactly 1 ticket","The answer is simply k + 1 (everyone from position 0 through k buys their single ticket)"],["Person k wants far more tickets than everyone else combined","Everyone else finishes quickly and contributes their full (small) ticket counts, while k's own large count dominates the total"]]}

items: Explicitly explaining the asymmetry (before-or-at k uses tickets[k], strictly-after k uses tickets[k]-1) and WHY it exists (k has already left by the time the line would cycle back to someone after them) demonstrates a complete understanding of the underlying round-robin mechanics.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: "A round-robin queue, but only ONE participant's finish time is needed" points toward computing each OTHER participant's direct contribution, rather than a full step-by-step simulation.

items: How would you find the finish time for EVERY person, not just person k? Repeating this O(n) computation for each of the n people would give O(n^2) total; a smarter combined approach might process all finish times together more efficiently, though this specific problem only ever asks for one.

How would you verify the -1 adjustment is correct without hand-deriving it? Trace a small concrete example (like tickets=[2,3,2], k=2) by both the direct formula AND a full simulation, confirming they agree exactly, as demonstrated in this walkthrough.

What if a person could leave the line early (before finishing) under some condition? The formula would need to account for that early departure explicitly, likely requiring a more careful case-by-case adjustment or a return to simulation for that scenario.

A round-robin queue simulation problem where recognizing a DIRECT mathematical shortcut (avoiding the literal simulation) is the key insight, distinguishing it from other queue-based problems in this category that genuinely require step-by-step processing.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text:
Brute force: O(n * max(tickets)) time, O(n) space.
Optimized (direct per-person contribution formula): O(n) time, O(1) space.

items: Pattern: Direct per-person contribution computation, replacing a round-robin queue simulation

Core Idea: Each person at or before k contributes min(their tickets, tickets[k]); each person after k contributes min(their tickets, tickets[k]-1), since k finishes before the line cycles back to them one final time
Time: O(n)
Space: O(1)
Most Important Observation: Someone positioned AFTER k misses out on k's very last round entirely, since k has already finished and left by the time the line would reach them again
Interview Difficulty: Easy
One-line memory trick: i<=k: add min(tickets[i], tickets[k]); i>k: add min(tickets[i], tickets[k]-1)
